implementerProof.how: Round two: the implement handoff now carries eleven proofs, all at the forward-merge head 9c20e8745947d1e43c4ca299de3da8af20d9b8f4. Every one was re-driven independently at that tree, not re-run from the implementer's rig: the same second DPoP/RFC 8693 client written from RFC 9449 and RFC 8693 with the Go standard library alone (ES256 JWS, RFC 7638 thumbprint, jti/htm/htu/iat/ath), never internal/broker/helper, against a freshly built live pair (packages/envoy/scripts/dev-broker.sh and packages/dispatch e2e/local-instance.ts) with a counting reverse proxy between Dispatch and the broker. Both failures of round one are answered: the branch no longer conflicts with main (gh pr view: mergeable MERGEABLE) and GitHub has started runs at the head, and the eleventh proof — the dev box token half of the revocation line the architect kept — is recorded and true: I drove a machine login by hand again (device authorization with an RFC 9101 request object and dpop_jkt, approved through agent-secrets-devrelay, the device code redeemed, then exchanged under session ada-devbox) and Dispatch accepted the token at t=+4.2 s and refused it 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE at t=+4.7 s after revoke-by-approver. This was a full round rather than a bare-gate re-check, because the forward merge moves the unchanged-diff fingerprint: main had moved 62 commits, the merge resolves packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/api/routes_table.go, packages/envoy/AGENTS.md and cmd/dispatch/README.md, and it renumbers the replay-store migration 0139_dpop_proofs to 0148_dpop_proofs.

proof.criterion: A caller presenting a broker-issued token is accepted, and Dispatch reports the session, the person and the project (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The live pair rebuilt at the forward-merge tree: packages/envoy/scripts/dev-broker.sh (real cmd/broker, real dev-oidc-issuer, its own Postgres database) and packages/dispatch `bun run dispatch:local` (real Go server, real Postgres with every migration applied, the production SPA build), driven by a DPoP client written from the RFCs with the Go standard library alone.
proof.command: dpopdrv exchange --subject-token-file $DEV_BROKER_DIR/exchange-token --session example-worker-session; then GET http://127.0.0.1:24917/api/v1/whoami under 'Authorization: DPoP <token>' with a proof carrying jti/htm/htu/iat/ath
proof.observed: 200 {"kind":"agent","owner":"ada@example.com","project":"EXAMPLE","service":null,"session":"example-worker-session"} — every field from the token, the request carrying no actor.
proof.negativeControl: The same token under Bearer → 401 UNAUTHORIZED; under DPoP with no proof → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; with the proof's ath dropped, with another token's ath, with htu naming http://evil.example, with typ jwt, with one jti presented twice, and with iat ten minutes either side of now → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID each; proved by a second ES256 key → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_KEY_MISMATCH.

proof.criterion: A call whose actor names a session the token does not is refused (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The same live pair: POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments with one broker token, varying the body's actor.
proof.command: POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments under DPoP three times: no actor; a matching session actor; an actor naming ses-not-mine
proof.observed: No actor → 201; the matching actor → 201; another session → 403 ACTOR_SESSION_MISMATCH 'this request's credential acts for session example-worker-session; its actor names another writer'.
proof.negativeControl: The two accepted halves in the same run, so the refusal is the mismatch and not the presence of an actor.

proof.criterion: A write to an object of a project the token does not cover is refused and names both projects; the same call against its own project succeeds; a write that belongs to no project is refused to a project-scoped token (INFRA-265).
proof.surface: The same live pair, with the token's own project (EXAMPLE) and the seed's CORE, one object of every addressing kind in each.
proof.command: Under one EXAMPLE-scoped token: POST /api/v1/issues/{EXAMPLE-1,CORE-1}/comments; PATCH /api/v1/issues/CORE-1; POST /api/v1/comments/{a CORE comment}/reply; POST /api/v1/asks/{a CORE ask}/resolve; POST /api/v1/artifacts/{a CORE document}/versions; POST /api/v1/projects/CORE/artifacts; POST /api/v1/issues with project CORE and with project EXAMPLE; POST /api/v1/projects; POST /api/v1/broadcasts
proof.observed: Its own project → 201 twice (a comment, and the issue create whose project the body names). All six CORE addresses → 403 PROJECT_SCOPE 'this request's credential may write project EXAMPLE; this write belongs to project CORE', one for each of the issue-key, comment-id, ask-id, artifact-id and project-key resolvers and for the issue create. POST /api/v1/projects and POST /api/v1/broadcasts → 403 PROJECT_SCOPE_DEPLOYMENT naming the route.
proof.negativeControl: In the same run a signed-in person's cookie created both projects and their issues: the check is a no-op for a credential that names no project. `go test ./internal/dispatch/api -run TestEveryMutatingRouteIsClassed` passes with its two sub-tests, which fail on a fixture holding an unclassed mutating row and on one classed as a project's write whose address names no object. The merge brought main's new mutating row POST /api/v1/projects/{key}/related, and the resolution classes it scopeProject, decided by the same /api/v1/projects/{key} resolver this proof drove at POST /api/v1/projects/CORE/artifacts.

proof.criterion: A project-scoped token reaches nothing it should not through a route classed as the calling session's or the deployment's (INFRA-265, read as an attacker).
proof.surface: The same live pair: the scopeSession rows a session caller can address.
proof.command: Under the EXAMPLE token: POST /api/v1/me/agent-tokens; POST /api/v1/agents/{another session}/messages
proof.observed: 403 HUMAN_ONLY for both: no path from a project-scoped pod token to an unscoped personal token, or into another session's conversation.
proof.negativeControl: The same writes succeed for the signed-in person in the instance's own seed, so the refusals are the caller's standing and not a broken route.

proof.criterion: A revoked token stops working within the cache's few seconds, and a refusal is never served from a cache — the exchanged-token half (INFRA-264, the architect's point 4).
proof.surface: The same live pair, with a counting reverse proxy between Dispatch and the broker, so every introspection Dispatch makes is observable from outside Dispatch.
proof.command: whoami (caches the affirmative answer at t=0), POST /v1/oauth/revoke at the broker as the dispatch caller, then whoami every half second
proof.observed: Accepted from t=+0.0 to t=+4.7 s, 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE at t=+5.2 s; the window cost two introspections. A refusal is never cached: one unknown token presented twice cost two introspections and answered 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE twice. The cache and its single flight measured the same way: five presentations of a fresh token within 1.5 s cost one introspection, a sixth after five seconds cost a second, and ten concurrent presentations of a fresh token cost exactly one with all ten answered 200.
proof.negativeControl: The same revocation presented by the introspection-only caller → 403 ACCOUNT_LACKS_POWER 'the caller "listener" may not call POST /v1/oauth/revoke', and whoami stayed 200 after it.

proof.criterion: A revoked token stops working within the cache's few seconds — the dev box token half (INFRA-264; the architect's point 4, now the implement handoff's eleventh proof).
proof.surface: The same live pair, driving a person's machine login by hand: POST /v1/oauth/device_authorization with an RFC 9101 request object (typ agent-secrets-request+jwt, a launcher_credential detail, login_hint ada@example.com) and dpop_jkt, approved with agent-secrets-devrelay machine-approve, the device code redeemed for the machine access token, then exchanged for a Dispatch token under session ada-devbox.
proof.command: POST /v1/oauth/token (token-exchange, subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token, session=ada-devbox); GET /api/v1/whoami; POST /v1/launcher-credentials/81ef5194-e36d-4fd8-86e3-52d43c510b32/revoke-by-approver as the dispatch caller; then whoami every half second
proof.observed: Introspection: {"active":true,"session":"ada-devbox","person":"ada@example.com","project_scope":"person","client_id":"dispatch-token-exchange"}, naming no project. whoami → 200 {"kind":"agent","owner":"ada@example.com","project":null,"service":null,"session":"ada-devbox"}, and that token wrote CORE-1 and EXAMPLE-1 (201 each), the documented rule for a person-scoped token. The revoke answered {"state":"revoked"}; Dispatch accepted at t=+4.2 s and refused 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE at t=+4.7 s.
proof.negativeControl: The same revoke-by-approver presented by the introspection-only caller → 403 ACCOUNT_LACKS_POWER naming that caller and that route, with the token still accepted afterwards.

proof.criterion: The document editor's live connection no longer accepts a shared bearer, and a person's own connection still edits (INFRA-264, INFRA-265's browser half).
proof.surface: The live Dispatch: GET /ws/doc/{document} upgraded three ways with curl --http1.1, and the repository's own browser suite in a real Chromium against the production SPA build.
proof.command: Upgrade /ws/doc/{EXAMPLE-1's spec} with 'Authorization: Bearer e2e-token' and the old X-Dispatch-Actor header, and with a signed-in person's cookie; then `bunx playwright test --config e2e/playwright.config.ts --project=chromium e2e/doc.e2e.ts e2e/collab-cursor.e2e.ts` against the same instance
proof.observed: The shared token → 401 Unauthorized; the person's cookie → 101 Switching Protocols. The browser suite: 17 of 17 rows passed in 2.0 m — two people editing one document live, their cursors, named versions, the diff, an agent edit landing in an open editor, reconnection after a dropped transport. `grep -rn 'X-Dispatch-Actor'` over the tree finds nothing outside packages/envoy/CHANGELOG.md.
proof.negativeControl: The same shared token on the HTTP API in the same run → 200 at /api/v1/whoami, so the socket's 401 is the deleted door and not a wrong token. (The first attempt of this suite failed 17 of 17 at browserType.launch: the forward merge moved Playwright's pin to chromium_headless_shell-1248, which this pod did not hold; `bunx playwright install chromium` fixed it and the suite then passed. That is the pod's browser cache, not the change.)

proof.criterion: Dispatch's unauthenticated path cannot spend the people's approval budget (plan P5), and the broker is never asked twice for one answer.
proof.surface: The same live pair with the counting proxy.
proof.command: Forty presentations of forty distinct unknown tokens from one source address, counting the introspections that reached the broker
proof.observed: 32 reached the broker (32 × 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE) and 8 were refused 401 BROKER_TOKEN_RATE_LIMITED without the broker being asked at all.
proof.negativeControl: The honest caller is unaffected in the same stack: ten concurrent presentations of one live token cost one introspection and all ten answered 200.

proof.criterion: A broker outage refuses a broker-token caller rather than quietly unscoping it (the project check resolves the caller itself, so this is where it could fail open).
proof.surface: The same live pair with cmd/broker stopped.
proof.command: With the broker killed: GET /api/v1/whoami; POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments; POST /api/v1/issues/CORE-1/comments; POST /api/v1/projects — all under a token minted before the outage
proof.observed: 503 BROKER_UNAVAILABLE 'the secrets broker cannot be reached; try again in a minute' on every one, the write to its own project included: no write runs unscoped while the broker is down.
proof.negativeControl: In the same outage the shared token and a person's cookie both answered 200 at /api/v1/whoami, so the 503 is the broker-token branch alone.

proof.criterion: An open stream re-resolves its caller without replaying the proof, and a multipart body is not eaten by the token reader (the two things the implement handoff argues rather than drives).
proof.surface: The live Dispatch: a /ws/live socket held open under a broker token, and a multipart artifact upload under one.
proof.command: A WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:24917/ws/live with 'Authorization: DPoP <token>' and one proof, held 45 s (three fifteen-second heartbeats); and POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/artifacts as multipart/form-data under DPoP
proof.observed: The socket stayed open the whole 45 s and took two frames, never closed; the multipart upload answered 201 with the artifact recorded.
proof.negativeControl: The same socket's upgrade with no DPoP proof is refused, as the whoami controls above show for every route; and the document socket under the same token is 401, since it takes a person's cookie alone.

proof.criterion: A pod cannot obtain a token naming a session of another issue, a relaunch is never refused, and a fixed-session account survives a rollout (INFRA-382); an account listed only for introspection is refused the relay routes by name and no row may be added without a power (INFRA-401); account authentication reads the issuer's keys through the cache that bounds a forged flood, a legitimate caller is answered throughout one, and a rotation is picked up (INFRA-402); the replay store's migration applies in its new place.
proof.surface: The real cmd/broker binary and the packages' own suites against a real Postgres, at the merged tree.
proof.command: go test -run 'TestEveryMutatingRouteIsClassed|TestAProjectScopedTokenWritesOnlyItsOwnProject' ./internal/dispatch/api; go test -run 'TestEveryAccountRouteDeclaresItsPower|Flood' ./internal/broker/api; go test ./internal/oidc/... ./internal/brokertoken/...; go test -run 'TestAPodWritesOnlyUnderASessionRegisteredForIt|TestAListedAccountReachesOnlyItsOwnRoutes' ./cmd/broker; go test -tags multiprocess -run TestAFixedSessionNameAcrossARollout ./cmd/broker; go test ./internal/dispatch/store/...
proof.observed: All pass at the merged tree: internal/dispatch/api 7.6 s, internal/broker/api 4.8 s, internal/oidc 15.7 s, internal/brokertoken 15.1 s, cmd/broker 33.6 s, cmd/broker multiprocess 11.0 s, internal/dispatch/store 491.0 s — the last of which runs every migration, so 0148_dpop_proofs applies in the place the merge moved it to.
proof.negativeControl: TestAForgedAccountTokenFloodCostsAFetchEachWithoutTheKeyCachesMinimumRefresh is the key cache's control and passes; TestEveryAccountRouteDeclaresItsPower fails on a row that declares no power and api.Register refuses to mount such a table; TestEveryMutatingRouteIsClassed's two sub-tests fail on an unclassed mutating row and on an unresolvable project row.

environment.note: The issue pod has no Docker, no root and no Postgres of its own; the harness is the unpacked-Debian Postgres 17 at /legion/harness (docs/solutions/testing/the-real-dispatch-stack-runs-inside-a-legion-pod-with-no-postgres-no-docker-and-no-root-INFRA-42.md). Three pod limits bear on what can be driven, none a defect of this change: gVisor answers SO_PEERPIDFD 'protocol not available', so agent-secrets-helper refuses every local client and a machine login must be driven as its four HTTP steps; playwright's webkit and firefox cannot be installed, so only chromium rows run, and the forward merge moved playwright's chromium pin, which needed `bunx playwright install chromium` in this pod before the document rows would launch at all; and the browser cache lives under /legion/scratch, the issue volume, not the container's own disk.
